claims.claim: LTA-containing membranes of S. pneumoniae sediment at low centrifugal speed.
claims.source: Since we were able to fluorescently label TA, we thought it would allow simpler in-gel analysis. WT cells were cultured over two generations in C-medium devoid of choline but supplemented with 200 µM aCho. Cells having thus metabolically incorporated aCho were lyzed by overnight digestion of the cell wall with lysozyme, mutanolysin and recombinant LytA. The aCho was coupled to a DBCO-fluorescent Alexa dye (AF488) by SPAAC click reaction during the lysis incubation. The lysates were then cleared of debris by a low-speed centrifugation at 10,000 × g, and ultracentrifugation of the supernatant at 100,000 × g was subsequently performed to separate the membrane from the soluble fraction. Since at this stage the TA were fluorescently labeled, we were surprised to find more fluorescence in the low-speed pellet than in the pellet resulting from the ultracentrifugation.
claims.evidence: This is an unexpected experimental observation from the fractionation procedure.

claims.claim: The pattern expected from labeled WTA is a set of poorly resolved bands with low electrophoretic mobility.
claims.source: Analysis of the soluble fraction (the supernatant) by SDS–PAGE showed the pattern expected from labeled WTA migrating as a set of poorly resolved bands with low electrophoretic mobility, as in typical Alcian blue-stained gels (Flores-Kim et al., 2019; Flores-Kim et al., 2022; Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental gel electrophoresis data shown in Figure 4A and citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The pattern expected from labeled LTA is a ladder of well-resolved bands with a greater electrophoretic mobility than the WTA.
claims.source: The pattern expected from labeled LTA, a ladder of well-resolved bands with a greater electrophoretic mobility than the WTA, was observed chiefly in the low-speed pellet.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental gel electrophoresis data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: 2 min at 20,000 × g were sufficient to sediment most of the LTA.
claims.source: Centrifugation of cells lysates with labeled TA at different speeds confirmed that 2 min at 20,000 × g were sufficient to sediment most of the LTA (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental centrifugation data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: The total amount of TA choline residues per cell is about (12.5 ± 1.5) × 10^6.
claims.source: The total amount of TA choline residues per cell can therefore be estimated to be about (12.5 ± 1.5) × 106.
claims.evidence: This is calculated from experimental titration data shown in Figure 4B, C.

claims.claim: The number of TA molecules per cell is about 10^6.
claims.source: Assuming that the major species of TA consists of 6 repeating units, as determined previously (Gisch et al., 2013; Bui et al., 2012), with each unit comprising about two choline residues, the number of TA molecules per cell is about 106.
claims.evidence: This is calculated from experimental titration data and assumptions about TA structure, with citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Labeled choline residues incorporated into LTAs account for 15 ± 5% of the TA choline residues.
claims.source: Labeled choline residues incorporated into LTAs were found to account for 15 ± 5% of the TA choline residues.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental quantification from gel electrophoresis data.

claims.claim: LTA and WTA represent roughly 15 and 85% of pneumococcal TA, respectively.
claims.source: Assuming that the amount of polymerized TA precursors is negligible, and that size distribution is similar for LTA and WTA, LTA and WTA represent roughly 15 and 85% of pneumococcal TA, respectively.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on experimental quantification data with stated assumptions.

claims.claim: Longer species of LTA can be observed at later stages of growth.
claims.source: Remarkably, longer species of LTA can be observed at later stages of growth (Figure 5A, B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental gel electrophoresis data shown in Figure 5A, B, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The most abundant form of LTA consists of 6 repeating units during exponential phase.
claims.source: Assuming that the most abundant form consists of 6 repeating units (Gisch et al., 2013), the 5- and 7-unit species are the next most abundant species, and traces of the 8- and 9-unit species can be detected during the exponential phase of growth.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental gel electrophoresis data and citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: During late culture phases, longer LTA species become more abundant with up to 17 identifiable units.
claims.source: Later during the culture, although the 6-unit species remains the most abundant and the 5-unit is detected at level comparable as earlier in the culture, longer species become more abundant with up to 17 identifiable units.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental gel electrophoresis data shown in Figure 5A, B.

claims.claim: The size distribution of LTA in late culture appears to be bimodal with a first group of species consisting of 5–11 units, and a second group of longer forms where the most abundant one contains 15 units.
claims.source: Surprisingly, the size distribution appears to be bimodal with a first group of species consisting of 5–11 units, and a second group of longer forms where the most abundant one contains 15 units.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental gel electrophoresis data shown in Figure 5A, B.

claims.claim: There was no significant difference in LTA length distribution between WT and ΔlytA strains.
claims.source: There was no significant difference between the strains with and without LytA (Figure 5A, B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental gel electrophoresis data comparing the two strains.

claims.claim: Although WT cells lyse, their WTA and LTA are not degraded and remain unchanged in the medium.
claims.source: The ΔlytA did not lyse spontaneously, but a similar amount of TA with the same distribution was obtained from the lysing lytA+ culture. Thus, although the WT cells lyse, their WTA and LTA are not degraded and remain unchanged in the medium.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on experimental gel electrophoresis data comparing lysing and non-lysing cultures.

claims.claim: No modification of the pulse-labeled TA could be detected during the chase time in WT cells.
claims.source: We also monitored the fate of the labeled species during a chase period of further growth following a 5-min labeling pulse of WT cells, mirroring the dSTORM observations. No modification of the pulse-labeled TA could be detected during the chase time, whether the growth, labeling pulse and chase were performed in BHI or C-medium and supplemented with yeast extract (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental gel electrophoresis data from pulse-chase experiments shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Labeled TA found in the pellet of ΔtacL lysates are indistinguishable from LTA when analyzed by gel electrophoresis.
claims.source: WTA and LTA were examined in a strain devoid of TacL, which is thought to be responsible for the attachment of LTA to membrane glycolipids (Figure 6A). Labeled TA were found in the pellet, and when analyzed by gel electrophoresis were indistinguishable from LTA.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental gel electrophoresis data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: The sedimented TA in ΔtacL cells are membrane-bound precursors still attached to the undecaprenyl pyrophosphate lipid carrier.
claims.source: After double checking that the strain was indeed deleted for the tacL gene, we hypothesized that the sedimented TA could be membrane-bound precursors still attached to the undecaprenyl pyrophosphate lipid carrier.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on experimental observations and subsequent biochemical characterization.

claims.claim: Pulse-labeled LTA-like bands disappeared during a chase in ΔtacL cells.
claims.source: In support of this idea, pulse-labeled LTA-like bands disappeared during a chase (Figure 6B), as would be expected if these compounds were precursors being transformed into WTA.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental gel electrophoresis data from pulse-chase experiments shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: The pyrophosphate linkage in TA precursors is labile at low pH and high temperature.
claims.source: The pyrophosphate linkage in the PG precursor lipid II is labile at low pH and high temperature (Higashi et al., 1967). Reasoning that the same should be true for the TA precursor, we incubated the sedimented fraction from the WT and ΔtacL strain at 99°C at either pH 8 or pH 4.2. The TA sedimented from the ΔtacL lysate were degraded at both pH, whereas those from the parental strain were still detected (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C and citation to a previous study on lipid II.

claims.claim: P. aeruginosa colicin M can hydrolyze labeled sedimented TA from ΔtacL cells.
claims.source: P. aeruginosa colicin M could indeed hydrolyze labeled sedimented TA from ΔtacL cells, whereas it was inactive on labeled LTA from WT cells (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: TacL is the glycosyltransferase responsible for the attachment of TA to the membrane glycolipids.
claims.source: The combined results show that TacL is indeed the glycosyltransferase responsible for the attachment of TA to the membrane glycolipids (Heß et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data from this study and citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: In the absence of TacL, membrane-bound TA remain present in abundance in the form of undecaprenyl-pyrophosphate-attached precursors.
claims.source: Moreover, they reveal that in the absence of TacL, membrane-bound TA remain present in abundance in the form of undecaprenyl-pyrophosphate-attached precursors.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data from biochemical characterization of the ΔtacL strain.

claims.claim: LTA in the WT strain and membrane-bound precursors in the ΔtacL strain are located on the outer side of the plasma membrane.
claims.source: LTA in the WT strain or membrane-bound precursors in the ΔtacL strain were equally labeled before and after lysis, like WTA. In contrast, cytoplasmic azido-phosphocholine was only labeled after lysis, demonstrating that the DBCO-AF488 dye is membrane impermeant. These observations are in agreement with the polymerization of TA taking place at the cell surface (Gibson and Veening, 2023).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data from click-labeling before and after lysis, shown in Figure 6F, and citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: In the WT strain, labeled WTA represent ~80% of the total labeled TA.
claims.source: In the WT strain, labeled WTA in this particular experiment was found to represent ~80% of the total labeled TA, whereas in the ΔlytR strain, this proportion decreased to ~40%.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental densitometry data from gel electrophoresis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: In the ΔlytR strain, labeled WTA represent ~40% of the total labeled TA.
claims.source: In the WT strain, labeled WTA in this particular experiment was found to represent ~80% of the total labeled TA, whereas in the ΔlytR strain, this proportion decreased to ~40%.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental densitometry data from gel electrophoresis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The ratio of WTA to LTA amounts is decreased about five to sevenfold in the absence of LytR.
claims.source: Thus, the ratio of WTA to LTA amounts is decreased about five to sevenfold in the absence of LytR.
claims.evidence: This is calculated from experimental densitometry data.

claims.claim: The thinning of the periplasmic space and disappearance of the granular layer in strains with diminished amounts of either WTA or LTA support Erickson's hypothesis that a periplasmic space is maintained by the physical properties of WTA and LTA.
claims.source: The thinning of the periplasmic space and disappearance of the granular layer in strains with diminished amounts of either WTA (ΔlytR) or LTA (ΔtacL) support Erickson's hypothesis that a periplasmic space is maintained by the physical properties of WTA emanating from the PG layer and LTA springing from the membrane Erickson, 2021.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on experimental CEMOVIS data and citation to Erickson's hypothesis.

claims.claim: The appearance of the cell envelope of S. gordonii and S. pneumoniae are similar by CEMOVIS, despite different TA compositions.
claims.source: In this framework, it is also striking that the appearance of the cell envelope of S. gordonii (Zuber et al., 2006) and S. pneumoniae are so similar, despite the fact that the composition of their TA are very different (Denapaite et al., 2012; Park et al., 2020; Lima et al., 2019), lending credence to a fundamental function of TA stemming from their general physico-chemical properties, rather than from specific molecular interactions.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of CEMOVIS data with citations to previous studies on TA composition.

claims.claim: The surface density of LTA in S. pneumoniae is about 3.3 × 10^16 molecule⋅m^−2 or one LTA chain per 30 nm^2.
claims.source: The surface density of LTA would therefore be 3.3 × 1016 molecule⋅m–2 or one LTA chain per 30 nm2.
claims.evidence: This is calculated from experimental titration data and geometric assumptions about cell size.

claims.claim: The density of LTA in S. pneumoniae is lower than that calculated for LTA from Staphylococcus aureus (one chain per 5 nm^2).
claims.source: This density value is lower than that of one chain per 5 nm2 calculated for LTA from Staphylococcus aureus based on the ratio of LTA to membrane lipids (Erickson, 2021).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison with a calculation cited from a previous study.

claims.claim: The density values of LTA in S. pneumoniae and S. aureus are probably compatible with the polymer brush model.
claims.source: Although both density values are rough estimates, they likely require volume exclusion to accommodate TA chains at the membrane surface and are probably compatible with the polymer brush model.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative inference based on calculated density values and theoretical models.

claims.claim: In WT cells, production of WTA and LTA are competing pathways that rapidly consume the undecaprenyl-linked polymerized TA precursors.
claims.source: It is most likely that in WT cells, production of WTA and LTA are competing pathways as the two polymers share the same composition, that rapidly consumes the undecaprenyl-linked polymerized TA precursors, whereas these precursors accumulate in the ΔtacL strain (Figure 6B–E).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data from pulse-chase experiments and biochemical characterization.

claims.claim: The slower turnover of undecaprenyl-linked TA in the ΔtacL strain allows the cell wall incorporation of labeled WTA during the chase, several minutes after the aCho has been removed from the medium.
claims.source: The slower turnover of the undecaprenyl-linked TA in the ΔtacL strain allows the cell wall incorporation of labeled WTA during the chase, several minutes after the aCho has been removed from the medium.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on experimental dSTORM and gel electrophoresis data from pulse-chase experiments.

claims.claim: The observation by CEMOVIS that the cell envelope architecture is altered in ΔtacL cells indicates that undecaprenyl-attached TA precursors cannot fully replace the function of mature LTA.
claims.source: The observation by CEMOVIS that the cell envelope architecture is altered in ΔtacL cells, with a thinner periplasmic space devoid of granular layer (Figure 1), indicates that if some functional replacement occurs, it is not complete.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on experimental CEMOVIS data.

claims.claim: The physical properties of the undecaprenyl chain may restrict the presence and function of undecaprenyl-linked TA precursors to sites of cell wall assembly.
claims.source: It has been proposed previously that the physical properties of the undecaprenyl chain underlie the localization of the PG precursor lipid II at the sites of cell wall assembly, which occurs at sites of maximal membrane curvature (Calvez et al., 2019). The same reasoning would restrict the presence, and thus the function, of the undecaprenyl-linked TA precursors to sites of cell wall assembly were they can be incorporated into WTA or true LTA.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative inference based on analogy to lipid II localization, with citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: It is likely that most of the LTA-containing membranes were unknowingly discarded in previous studies during a clarification step of cell lysates.
claims.source: However, it is likely that most of the LTA-containing membranes were unknowingly discarded in these experiments during a clarification step of cell lysates, suggesting that the reported ratio of LTA to WTA were underestimated.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the discovery of low-speed sedimentation of LTA-containing membranes.

claims.claim: The reported ratio of LTA to WTA in previous studies were likely underestimated.
claims.source: However, it is likely that most of the LTA-containing membranes were unknowingly discarded in these experiments during a clarification step of cell lysates, suggesting that the reported ratio of LTA to WTA were underestimated.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the discovery of low-speed sedimentation of LTA-containing membranes.

results.result: CEMOVIS imaging reveals a periplasmic space in S. pneumoniae with a granular layer that is altered in ΔtacL and ΔlytR mutants. The periplasmic space thickness is significantly reduced by 34±5% in ΔtacL and 29±5% in ΔlytR strains, and the granular layer disappears in both mutants. Cell wall thickness is also reduced by 17±5% in ΔtacL and 36±4% in ΔlytR strains.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C52-C61 are well-supported by quantitative CEMOVIS measurements presented in Figure 2 and Table 1, with statistical analysis showing significant differences. The disappearance of the granular layer (C54) and thickness reductions (C55, C56, C59, C60) are documented with standard errors and statistical tests. The negative result from freeze-substitution TEM (C62) provides important methodological context.

results.result: The structural changes in the periplasmic space upon deletion of TA attachment genes support the hypothesis that TA play a role in maintaining the periplasmic space in Gram-positive bacteria.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C8, and C99 are supported by the CEMOVIS data showing structural alterations in ΔtacL and ΔlytR strains. The inference that TA maintain the periplasmic space is reasonable given the quantitative changes observed, though the mechanism remains to be fully elucidated. The support for Erickson's hypothesis (C99) is appropriately qualified as the data are consistent with but do not definitively prove the polymer brush model.

results.result: TA insertion occurs primarily at mid-cell in all three strains (WT, ΔtacL, ΔlytR), but pulse-chase experiments reveal different dynamics. In WT cells, labeled TA show separated banded patterns after chase, while in ΔtacL cells, labeled TA spread over the entire new cell surface generated during the chase period.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C72 are supported by dSTORM imaging data shown in Figure 3 and supplementary figures. The mid-cell localization is clearly demonstrated, and the pulse-chase experiments show distinct patterns between WT and ΔtacL strains. The interpretation that these patterns reflect WTA localization (C68) is reasonably inferred from sacculi preparations, though some heterogeneous surface labeling complicates interpretation.

results.result: LTA-containing membranes of S. pneumoniae sediment at low centrifugal speed (20,000×g for 2 min), allowing separation from soluble WTA by a simple centrifugation method. LTA appear as a ladder of well-resolved bands with higher electrophoretic mobility than WTA.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C76 are well-supported by experimental gel electrophoresis data in Figure 4A showing clear separation of LTA and WTA by low-speed centrifugation. This is an unexpected but reproducible finding confirmed by multiple experiments. The electrophoretic patterns match expectations from previous studies using different methods, and NMR analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 5) confirms the identity of the sedimented material as LTA.

results.result: A novel fluorescent labeling method enables quantitative analysis of TA. Titration experiments show approximately 12.5±1.5×10^6 TA choline residues per cell, corresponding to about 10^6 TA molecules per cell. LTA represent approximately 15±5% of total TA, with WTA comprising the remaining 85%.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C11 and C77-C80 are supported by titration experiments shown in Figure 4B,C with appropriate quantification and error analysis. The calculation from choline residues to TA molecules (C78) relies on reasonable assumptions about TA structure from previous studies. The LTA:WTA ratio determination (C79-C80) is based on densitometry with stated assumptions about size distribution and negligible precursor amounts, which are reasonable but introduce some uncertainty.

results.result: LTA length changes during growth phases, with longer species (up to 17 repeating units) appearing in stationary phase, showing a bimodal distribution. The 6-unit species remains most abundant throughout growth. No modification of pulse-labeled TA occurs during chase in WT cells, and LTA are not degraded during autolysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C87 are supported by gel electrophoresis data in Figure 5 comparing exponential, stationary, and lysis phases. The bimodal distribution (C84) is clearly visible in the densitometry profiles. The comparison between WT and ΔlytA strains (C85) and the pulse-chase stability (C87) are well-documented. However, the mechanism underlying the bimodal distribution and length changes remains unexplained.

results.result: The ΔtacL mutant accumulates membrane-bound TA precursors attached to undecaprenyl pyrophosphate rather than mature LTA. These precursors are labile at low pH and high temperature, sensitive to colicin M hydrolysis, and disappear during chase experiments as they are converted to WTA.
results.evaluation: Claims C13, C88-C94 are well-supported by multiple lines of biochemical evidence in Figure 6. The gel electrophoresis pattern (C88), pulse-chase disappearance (C90), pH/temperature lability (C91), colicin M sensitivity (C92), and resistance to the standard LTA isolation procedure all converge to support the identification of undecaprenyl-pyrophosphate-linked precursors. This confirms TacL's role as the glycosyltransferase (C93) and reveals precursor accumulation in its absence (C94).

results.result: LTA in WT cells and membrane-bound TA precursors in ΔtacL cells are located on the outer side of the plasma membrane, consistent with TA polymerization occurring at the cell surface.
results.evaluation: Claim C95 is supported by click-labeling experiments before and after lysis (Figure 6F) showing that LTA/precursors are labeled equally in both conditions, while cytoplasmic azido-phosphocholine is only labeled after lysis. This demonstrates membrane impermeability of the DBCO-AF488 reagent and external localization of TA. The conclusion is consistent with cited work on TA polymerization.

results.result: In ΔlytR cells, the proportion of WTA decreases from ~80% to ~40% of total labeled TA, representing a five to sevenfold decrease in the WTA:LTA ratio compared to WT.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C98 are supported by densitometry analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1. The quantification is straightforward and the calculation of the ratio change is correct. However, the authors note that ΔlytR cells were harvested at different growth phases than WT, which could confound the interpretation since LTA length changes with growth phase (as shown in Figure 5).

results.result: The similar appearance of cell envelopes in S. gordonii and S. pneumoniae by CEMOVIS, despite different TA compositions, suggests a fundamental function of TA based on general physico-chemical properties rather than specific molecular interactions.
results.evaluation: Claim C100 is supported by comparison of CEMOVIS data with previous studies and citations documenting different TA compositions. This is a reasonable inference that supports the polymer brush model hypothesis. However, this is a comparative observation rather than direct experimental evidence, and the number of species compared is limited.

results.result: The calculated surface density of LTA in S. pneumoniae is approximately 3.3×10^16 molecules·m^-2 (one chain per 30 nm^2), which is lower than S. aureus but likely compatible with the polymer brush model requiring volume exclusion.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C103 are supported by calculations based on the titration data and geometric assumptions about cell size. The calculation methodology is sound, though it relies on approximations (spherical cell shape, average surface area). The comparison to S. aureus (C102) appropriately cites previous work. The conclusion about compatibility with the polymer brush model (C103) is appropriately qualified as speculative.

results.result: In WT cells, WTA and LTA production are competing pathways that rapidly consume undecaprenyl-linked precursors. In ΔtacL cells, slower precursor turnover allows continued WTA incorporation during chase. The altered cell envelope architecture in ΔtacL cells indicates that undecaprenyl-attached precursors cannot fully replace mature LTA function.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C107 are supported by the pulse-chase dSTORM data (Figure 3) and gel electrophoresis (Figure 6B). The inference about competing pathways (C104) and slower turnover (C105) reasonably explains the observed labeling patterns. The conclusion that precursors cannot fully replace LTA (C106) is supported by CEMOVIS showing altered architecture. The speculation about undecaprenyl chain restricting precursor localization (C107) is appropriately qualified and based on analogy to lipid II.

results.result: Previous studies likely underestimated the LTA:WTA ratio because LTA-containing membranes were unknowingly discarded during low-speed clarification steps.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C109 are reasonable inferences based on the discovery of low-speed sedimentation of LTA-containing membranes. The comparison with previous fractionation methods (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) supports this interpretation. However, this is a retrospective inference about other studies' methods rather than direct evidence, and the magnitude of underestimation in previous work is not quantified.

results.result: Background information on TA structure, biosynthesis, and function in Gram-positive bacteria, with specific details about S. pneumoniae TA composition, the role of choline-binding proteins, and the biosynthetic pathway involving TacF, TarP, LytR, and TacL.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C51 represent established knowledge and literature citations providing context for the study. These are appropriately cited to previous work and represent accurate summaries of the field. Some claims involve speculation (C5, C24, C35) or inference (C21, C51) that are appropriately qualified. These background claims are not primary results of this study but provide essential context.

results.result: CEMOVIS imaging reveals a periplasmic space in S. pneumoniae with a granular layer that is altered in ΔtacL and ΔlytR mutants. The periplasmic space thickness is significantly reduced by ~34% in ΔtacL and ~29% in ΔlytR strains, and the granular layer disappears in both mutants. Cell wall thickness is also reduced in both mutants, more so in ΔlytR (~36%) than ΔtacL (~17%). These findings support the hypothesis that both LTA and WTA participate in maintaining the periplasmic space.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm these findings. The editor states the study 'make[s] clever use of electron microscopy...to interrogate the role of teichoic acids in supporting the maintenance of the periplasmic region' and that 'findings are solid.' Reviewer 1 notes 'advanced electron microscopy approach was used. This also showed a likely role for both wall and lipo-teichoic acids in maintaining the periplasm.' Reviewer 3 states the study 'shows an interesting role for TAs in maintaining a 'periplasmic space' in Gram positives' and calls it 'an important piece of work.' No concerns were raised about the CEMOVIS data or the conclusions about periplasmic space maintenance.

results.result: LTA-containing membranes sediment at low centrifugal speed (20,000 × g for 2 min), contrary to expectations. Gel electrophoresis shows WTA migrate as poorly resolved bands with low mobility in the soluble fraction, while LTA appear as a ladder of well-resolved bands with greater mobility in the low-speed pellet.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 raises significant concerns about this finding. They question whether 'the pellet recovered at low speeds [is] not just some of the membrane that would sediment at this speed with or without LTA' and request controls using membrane proteins and the tacL mutant. They also note that 'enzymatic digestion of the cell wall and then sedimentation will allow cell wall associated proteins (and other material) to become bound to the membranes and potentially effect sedimentation properties,' requesting physical breakage experiments. In revision comments, Reviewer 1 notes that after physical breakage 'membrane proteins sediment at high speed (rather than low speed)' and states 'the sedimentation properties of membranes containing LTA are likely dependent on the way in which the cells are lysed,' requesting qualification of statements about this finding.

results.result: Using the novel metabolic labeling method, the authors quantified approximately 12.5 ± 1.5 × 10^6 TA choline residues per cell, corresponding to ~10^6 TA molecules per cell. LTA account for 15 ± 5% of TA choline residues, meaning LTA and WTA represent roughly 15% and 85% of pneumococcal TA, respectively.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 raises concerns about the validity of this quantification in light of the precursor accumulation findings. They state: 'If, as stated, most of the LTA-like bands are actually precursor then how can the quantification of LTA stand as stated in the text? The 'Titration of Cellular TA' section should be re-evaluated or removed?' They also note 'if you compare Fig. 6C WT extract incubated at RT and 110°C it seems like a large decrease in amount of material at the higher temperature. Thus, the WT has a lot of precursors in the membrane? This needs to be quantified.' These concerns suggest the quantification may be confounded by the presence of undecaprenyl-linked precursors.

results.result: LTA length changes during growth phases. During exponential phase, the most abundant form consists of 6 repeating units with 5- and 7-unit species also present. During late culture phases, longer species become more abundant (up to 17 units), with a bimodal distribution showing peaks at 5-11 units and around 15 units. No significant difference was observed between WT and ΔlytA strains, and pulse-labeled TA showed no modification during chase in WT cells.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not raise concerns about these findings regarding LTA length distribution during growth phases. The editor notes the findings are 'solid' and Reviewer 1 acknowledges the manuscript 'could be an important addition to the field' after technical issues were addressed. The lack of specific critique of these growth phase observations, combined with general positive assessments, suggests acceptance of these claims.

results.result: In ΔtacL cells, labeled TA found in the pellet are indistinguishable from LTA by gel electrophoresis but are actually membrane-bound precursors still attached to undecaprenyl pyrophosphate. These precursors disappear during pulse-chase experiments, are labile to low pH and high temperature, can be hydrolyzed by colicin M, and are located on the outer side of the plasma membrane. This confirms TacL as the glycosyltransferase responsible for LTA attachment to membrane glycolipids.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 expresses confusion about the relationship between these findings and other results, asking 'What is the difference between this and Fig. 5B, where the bands do not disappear? Fig. 5C is the WT and was only pulse labelled for 5 min and so would one not expect the LTA-like bands to disappear as in 6B?' This suggests uncertainty about the interpretation of precursor dynamics. Additionally, the concerns about quantification (point 5 in the review) directly relate to the implications of precursor accumulation, with the reviewer questioning whether 'most of the LTA-like bands are actually precursor.' While the biochemical characterization is not directly challenged, the functional interpretation and its impact on other conclusions remains uncertain.

results.result: In the WT strain, labeled WTA represent ~80% of total labeled TA, while in the ΔlytR strain this proportion decreases to ~40%. The ratio of WTA to LTA amounts is decreased about five to sevenfold in the absence of LytR.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly critiques the evidence for this claim, stating 'A single lane on a gel is not very convincing as to the role of LytR. Here, and throughout the manuscript, wherever statements concerning levels of material are made, quantification needs to be done over appropriate numbers of repeats and with densitometry data shown in SI.' This indicates the reviewer finds the evidence insufficient and requests additional quantification and replication. The lack of reproducibility data undermines confidence in these specific quantitative claims.

results.result: dSTORM imaging shows TA insertion occurs at mid-cell in WT, ΔtacL, and ΔlytR strains, where PG is assembled. In WT cells, pulse-chase experiments show the expected separated banded pattern. In ΔtacL cells, labeled TA remain visible over the whole new cell surface during pulse and first 15 min of chase, with an unlabeled region appearing at mid-cell only after 35 min. The localization patterns are mostly those of WTA, as the distribution is preserved in sacculi preparations.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not raise specific concerns about the dSTORM localization findings. Reviewer 1 notes 'The labelling was coupled with super-resolution microscopy to be able to map the teichoic acids at the subcellular level' as a strength of the study. The editor describes the work as making 'clever use of electron microscopy and metabolic labelling' with 'solid' findings. The absence of critique of these specific localization results, combined with positive overall assessments, indicates reviewer acceptance.

results.result: The novel metabolic labeling method enabled in-gel analysis of cell fractions.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly praise the metabolic labeling approach. Reviewer 1 states 'the authors use a metabolic labelling approach to analyse the teichoic acids. This is a clear strength as this method cannot be used for most other well studied organisms.' Reviewer 3 notes the study 'provides new and improved methods to study TAs' and states it 'pioneers some new methods that will definitively move the field forward.' The editor calls the approach 'clever' and the findings 'solid.' These positive assessments indicate strong support for the methodological contribution.

results.result: Transmission electron microscopy analysis of sectioned stained freeze-substituted resin-embedded samples did not reveal measurable differences between the cell wall of the WT and mutant strains, in contrast to CEMOVIS.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge this negative control observation. The finding serves to validate the CEMOVIS approach by showing that conventional TEM does not reveal the same differences, which supports the specificity and value of the CEMOVIS method. Since reviewers accept the CEMOVIS findings and do not question this comparative observation, it is implicitly supported.

results.result: The appearance of the cell envelope of S. gordonii and S. pneumoniae are similar by CEMOVIS despite different TA compositions, suggesting a fundamental function of TA stemming from general physico-chemical properties. The surface density of LTA in S. pneumoniae is calculated as ~3.3 × 10^16 molecules·m^-2 (one chain per 30 nm^2), lower than S. aureus (one per 5 nm^2), but both values are probably compatible with the polymer brush model.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these comparative and theoretical interpretations. Reviewer 3 notes the study 'shows an interesting role for TAs in maintaining a 'periplasmic space' in Gram positives' and calls it 'an important piece of work,' suggesting acceptance of the broader functional interpretations. The lack of specific critique of these density calculations and comparative observations, combined with overall positive assessments, indicates acceptance.

results.result: In WT cells, WTA and LTA production are competing pathways that rapidly consume undecaprenyl-linked TA precursors. In ΔtacL, slower turnover allows cell wall incorporation of labeled WTA during chase. CEMOVIS shows that undecaprenyl-attached TA precursors cannot fully replace mature LTA function. The physical properties of the undecaprenyl chain may restrict precursors to sites of cell wall assembly.
results.evaluation: While reviewers do not directly challenge these mechanistic interpretations, Reviewer 1's concerns about the pulse-chase data (asking about differences between figures and the disappearance of bands) and about the quantification in light of precursor accumulation indirectly affect confidence in these mechanistic conclusions. The interpretation depends on the validity of the precursor characterization and dynamics, which have been questioned. However, the CEMOVIS observation that ΔtacL architecture is altered is accepted, supporting the claim that precursors cannot fully replace LTA.

results.result: It is likely that most LTA-containing membranes were unknowingly discarded in previous studies during clarification steps, suggesting reported LTA to WTA ratios were underestimated.
results.evaluation: This inference depends on the validity of the low-speed sedimentation finding, which Reviewer 1 has questioned extensively. The reviewer's revision comments note that 'the sedimentation properties of membranes containing LTA are likely dependent on the way in which the cells are lysed' and request qualification of statements about this. Since the basis for this claim (unusual sedimentation of LTA) is uncertain, the inference about previous studies is also uncertain.

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluations support the CEMOVIS findings (C52-C61) showing structural alterations in mutant strains. OpenEval emphasizes quantitative measurements with statistical analysis, while peer reviewers praise the 'clever use of electron microscopy' and call findings 'solid.' Both also address claims about periplasmic space maintenance (C6-C8, C99), though OpenEval separates these into R2 while peer review groups them together. Overall strong agreement on CEMOVIS data quality and conclusions.

OpenEval supports claims C7, C8, C99 about TA maintaining periplasmic space and consistency with polymer brush model, noting appropriate qualification. Peer review R1 also supports these claims as part of their broader acceptance of the periplasmic space findings, with reviewers explicitly affirming the 'role for both wall and lipo-teichoic acids in maintaining the periplasm.' Strong agreement on these interpretations.

OpenEval notes clear demonstration of mid-cell localization with some heterogeneous surface labeling complicating interpretation. Peer reviewers praise the metabolic labeling coupled with super-resolution microscopy as a strength, with no specific concerns raised. Strong agreement.

However, peer review expresses significant uncertainty, with Reviewer 1 questioning whether the pellet is just membrane that would sediment regardless, requesting controls and noting that sedimentation properties depend on lysis method. Major disagreement on validity of this finding.

However, the broader uncertainty about precursor dynamics in peer review may indirectly affect confidence in related findings.

Disagreement on sufficiency of evidence.

OpenEval notes this is comparative observation rather than direct evidence. Peer reviewers accept the broader functional interpretations without specific critique. Agreement on this inference.

Partial disagreement.

Peer review expresses uncertainty because this depends on the validity of low-speed sedimentation finding, which Reviewer 1 has questioned extensively, noting sedimentation properties depend on lysis method. Peer review R8 specifically praises the metabolic labeling methodology as a 'clear strength' and notes it 'pioneers some new methods that will definitively move the field forward.' Strong agreement on methodological contribution.

Peer review implicitly supports this by accepting CEMOVIS findings without questioning this comparative observation. Agreement on this negative control.
